titleEn: Come, let us sing to the LORD
progression: | Dm Gm | Dm A | Dm Gm | A Dm |
intro: Eleven verses, said on Friday evening as the first of the six psalms that open Kabbalat Shabbat, which in the common rites makes it the first line of Shabbat. It begins as an invitation and ends as an indictment, and the turn happens inside a single verse. For a learner it is the best page in the book for the cohortative, the let-us form of the verb: let us sing, let us shout, let us come before, let us bow, let us kneel, six of them in the first six verses, all first person plural, all built by adding an unstressed -a to the end. Learn the pattern here and you can read half the calls to worship in the Psalter.

stichs.en: Come, let us sing out to the LORD,
let us shout to the Rock of our salvation.

verses.summary: An invitation, not a command to an individual: every verb is first person plural, so the speaker is standing inside the group he is calling. The Rock is a title, not a comparison.

stichs.en: Let us come before His face with thanksgiving,
with songs let us shout to Him.

verses.summary: The verb means to meet someone by arriving first, to get there ahead. Worship here is not a response to a summons but an approach made on the worshipper's own initiative.

stichs.en: For the LORD is a great God,
and a great King above all gods.

verses.summary: The first reason given, and it is a comparative one. The other powers are not denied; they are ranked below.

stichs.en: In whose hand are the deep places of the earth,
and the peaks of the mountains are His.

verses.summary: Lowest and highest named in one breath, which is the standard biblical way of saying everything in between. Both extremes are handled by a hand.

stichs.en: The sea is His, and He made it,
and the dry land His hands formed.

verses.summary: Sea and dry land are the two halves of the third day of creation, taken in the same order. Ownership is argued from manufacture, not from conquest.

stichs.en: Come, let us bow down and bend low,
let us kneel before the LORD our Maker.

verses.summary: The second invitation answers the first. Verse 1 opened the mouth, this one puts the body on the floor, and three verbs of lowering are stacked with no conjunction between the last two.

stichs.en: For He is our God,
and we are the people of His pasture, the flock of His hand.
Today, if you would listen to His voice!

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm, and it falls mid-verse. Up to the flock of His hand the congregation is speaking about God; from the word today it is God speaking to the congregation, and the sentence is left unfinished.

stichs.en: Do not harden your heart as at Meribah,
as on the day of Massah in the wilderness,

verses.summary: The first thing the divine voice says is a prohibition, and it names a place rather than a sin. The audience is expected to know the story without being told it.

stichs.en: where your fathers tested Me, tried Me,
though they had seen My work.

verses.summary: Both verbs carry the object suffix -ni, me, so the testing is personal rather than abstract. The complaint is not that they doubted but that they doubted after seeing.

stichs.en: Forty years I was disgusted with a generation,
and I said, they are a people who stray in heart,
and they have not known My ways.

verses.summary: Forty years is the length of the wandering, so the whole desert period is compressed into one verb of divine feeling. Straying is diagnosed in the heart first and only then in conduct.

stichs.en: so I swore in My anger,
they shall never enter into My rest.

verses.summary: The psalm that began with an invitation ends with a door closed, and it closes on the word rest. Nothing is said about whether the sentence still stands, which is why the previous verses matter.

pardes.body: Two unequal halves. Verses 1 to 7a are a congregation talking itself into worship: sing, shout, come before, bow, kneel, with two reasons attached, that God outranks every other power and that God made the sea and the land. Then at {{7.8}}, today, the speaker changes without warning and God answers. The answer is a warning built entirely out of one episode in the wilderness, and it ends on an oath. Read the whole psalm aloud and the effect is deliberate: the invitation to worship is granted, and what worship turns out to consist of is being spoken to. The last word, My rest, is left hanging over people who have just been called the flock of His hand.

Two of the place names in verse 8 are verbs elsewhere. Exodus 17:7 says the place was called Massah and Meribah because the people quarrelled and because they tested the LORD, and this psalm puts the matching roots back to work: {{8.3}} is the quarrel word, and {{9.1}} in the next verse is the testing word. Naming the place is therefore also restating the charge. Two other words are genuinely uncertain. {{4.2}}, the deep places, comes from the root for searching out, so it means something like the parts that have to be explored, and {{4.4}}, rendered peaks here, is rare enough that translations range across heights, summits and treasures. {{10.2}}, rendered I was disgusted, is disputed between loathing and weariness. In verse 11 the word {{11.3}} literally means if, and standing after a verb of swearing it is the ordinary Hebrew way of making an oath negative, so if they enter means they shall not enter.

The single word {{7.8}}, today, is the most cited word in the psalm. The Talmud in tractate Sanhedrin gives the exchange in which the Messiah is asked when he is coming and answers today, and the answer is then explained by this verse: today, if you will listen to His voice. The condition, on that reading, is not a threat about the past but an open offer standing at every moment. The same verse also does liturgical work by dividing the congregation from the wilderness generation. The psalm says your fathers, not you, and then says do not harden your heart, so each generation hearing it is placed at the same fork the desert generation stood at and told the outcome is not settled.

This is the first of six psalms that open Kabbalat Shabbat, and the six are commonly counted against the six days of the week, so the week is handed over one psalm at a time before Shabbat is received. That count gives the last word of this psalm a second life. {{11.6}}, My rest, is the same noun family as the rest of the seventh day, so the sequence that ends with a generation shut out of rest is the sequence that opens the evening on which rest arrives. The two halves of the psalm then read as the two things the week does to a person: it invites, and it hardens. Verse 6 puts three verbs of lowering in a row with no room between them, which is the practical answer the psalm offers to the second of those.
